<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
The comment does a lot of useful forensic work. But its conclusion goes well beyond its evidence, and it leaves out the study that most directly answers its own question.

I checked the arithmetic:
- Each row of Table 2 is correct: 95.1/0.8, 98.4/0.859, and 95.4/0.861.
- The hours ratios are right: 34.6/40.3 = 0.859 and 34.8/40.4 = 0.861.
- The real-revenue figure is right: 1.014/1.041 ≈ −2.6%.

One hours figure doesn't reconcile, which I cover in section 3.

## What holds up

- **Attrition.** If seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule started, and six cited workload or output, the working paper's "chiefly for scheduling reasons" is a material misdescription. This is the comment's most important factual contribution.
- **Manager vs record-based output.** In 19 of 23 organisations, the manager's index exceeded the records. A one-sided sign test gives p ≈ 0.003, so that is very unlikely to be chance. The mean gap is 3.8 points.
- **Hours.** Actual hours fell about 14%, not 20%. This is consistent with Varden, where they fell 13% in case-processing.
- **Revenue and sector-generality.** Both critiques are correct. They match the points I raised about the Halden paper itself.

## 1. Table 2 changes the sample at every step

The four rows cover 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. So the drop from 23.4% to 10.8% mixes two things: the effect of the corrections, and the effect of switching to a different, non-random set of organisations. The data note admits this, but the abstract and conclusion attribute the whole drop to the corrections.

The clean comparison is within the 17 organisations: their manager index divided by 0.8, then record-based output divided by 0.8, then manager index divided by actual hours, then record-based output divided by actual hours. All of these can be computed from the microdata the authors already hold, and only this version actually decomposes the drop.

## 2. Attrition is said to be corrected, but isn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, and attrition is the first. Table 2 adjusts only output and hours. Nothing in it handles the nine organisations that withdrew.

The comment should either:
- bound the effect of the withdrawals, for example with worst-case imputation or Lee bounds; or
- say plainly that 10.8% is a survivors-only estimate that attrition would probably push lower.

Two related points:
- **The abstract's "four problems" are not all corrections to the gain.** Revenue is listed as one of the four problems that "account for most of the reported gain", but it plays no part in the per-hour calculation.
- **The timing needs a sentence of explanation.** The working paper described two months of preparation workshops. The comment says withdrawals came "in the first month and the second" after the schedule began. Readers need to know when the schedule actually started, so they can see the contradiction is real and not a difference in how months are counted.

## 3. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Scheduled time was 4 × 8 = 32 hours. Adding the reported extras:
- longer days: 4 × 0.7 = 2.8 hours
- work logged on the day off: 1.6 hours
- total: 36.4 hours per week

The comment reports 34.6. Working back from 34.6, the four main days come to 33.0 hours, or 8.25 a day. That is about 0.25 hours over schedule, not 0.7.

36.4 and 34.6 use the same digits, so this may be a transposition. That needs checking, because it changes the result:
- If 36.4 is correct, actual hours fell only about 10%, and every actual-hours row in Table 2 changes.
- If 34.6 is correct, the +0.7 hours a day figure is wrong.

## 4. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own numbers

After the corrections, an 11% gain remains. The only explanation offered for it is novelty, which is extrapolated from two points of a survey variable (section 5). The data note says the corrected estimates describe subsets, not the pilot as a whole. "Entirely an artifact" is therefore assertion, not finding, and adding "in our assessment" doesn't make it one.

More importantly, the comment uses Varden selectively. It calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions the case-processing stratum of the same trial. That stratum found output per actual hour up 12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months. It used exactly the methods this comment recommends:
- randomised controls,
- output from administrative records,
- actual hours from timesheets,
- a registered analysis plan.

The comment's corrected Halden figure of 10.8% lands almost exactly on that randomised estimate. The more natural reading of the evidence is that the per-hour gain in non-coverage work is real but about half the size pilots report. It is not zero.

## 5. The novelty argument is weak

- **Wrong variable.** Energy is a survey measure, not output. The Halden output index was collected monthly. The direct test is whether output per hour declined from month one to month six. The comment has the data and doesn't report it.
- **Arithmetic.** On the comment's own linear extrapolation, energy declines by 0.107 SD a month and reaches baseline at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." More fundamentally, a straight line through two points is a weak basis for any forecast.
- **It conflicts with Varden.** Varden's per-hour gain was measured at nine months, after the point where the comment's extrapolation says the novelty would have worn off.
- **The burden-of-proof sentence is rhetoric.** The data available bear on novelty in both directions, so the claim should rest on them.

## 6. The meetings critique misdescribes what Varden did

- **Not a selected subgroup.** The seven offices are all of Varden's treated case-processing offices. That is a pre-registered stratum, not a subgroup picked out afterwards.
- **Not collected after the results.** Varden says the calendar data were collected in month six, at managers' request. That was before the nine-month results were known.
- **Varden already made the comment's point.** Its authors said the correlation "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test. "It should not be cited as a mechanism" restates their own caveat as though it were a rebuttal.

There is also a logical problem for the comment's thesis. If the meetings explanation turns out to be right, it describes a real productivity gain that comes from removing low-value time. That would not be an artifact of measurement, selection or novelty.

## 7. Record-based output isn't automatically neutral

The comment treats records as the true measure. But "billable hours delivered" is one of the record types used. For professional-services firms that bill by the hour, billable hours partly measure input: they fall almost automatically when working time falls. Two things are needed:
- how each record-based index was built, including which baseline period it used;
- a sensitivity check that drops organisations whose output measure is billable hours.

Some of the 3.8-point gap could come from the measure itself rather than from optimistic managers.

## Smaller points

- **CPI as the deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue. Sector-level producer prices would be better. The direction of the conclusion (a real decline) would very likely survive the change.
- **Retail.** The 11.2% fall rests on three organisations. That is worth saying in the text. It would also help to say whether any of these three were among the three retail organisations that reverted.

## Bottom line

As forensic work, the comment is valuable. It shows misreported attrition, a systematic upward bias in manager-reported output, and an inflated hours denominator.

As a conclusion, it doesn't hold. "Entirely an artifact" isn't supported:
- the corrections leave an 11% gain,
- the attrition correction is promised in the abstract but never made,
- the hours figures don't reconcile,
- the novelty claim rests on a survey variable and a straight line through two points,
- the one randomised estimate of non-coverage work, which the comment omits, finds about the same gain.

A defensible version would say:

> Pilot-reported per-hour gains are overstated by roughly half. In work not tied to presence, a gain of around 10–12% is consistent with randomised evidence, and durability is untested. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output.

I can draft a reply to the comment, or a short note putting all three documents side by side, if either would help.
